newsitem.title: BELGIUM: CAMPION STRIKES RIGHT CHORD IN PORTRAIT OF A LADY.
newsitem.headline: CAMPION STRIKES RIGHT CHORD IN PORTRAIT OF A LADY.

text.p: Australian film director Jane Campion, whose Piano won many admirers for its strong portrayal of a woman's struggle for independence, has hit a similar chord in her latest work, Portrait of a Lady.

Based on the novel of the same name by Henry James, the film tracks the trials and tribulations of a young, wealthy and independantly-minded American woman, played by Nicole Kidman, whose vanities and innocence lead her into the clutches of a manipulative rake played by John Malkovich.

Kidman carries the role very well in the 140-minute film, managing to strike the right balance between strength and frailty in an era when women were only just starting to flex their muscles against being treated as male possessions.
Malkovich slips easily into a role that has become his trademark, reprising -- almost down to the gesture -- the part he played in Dangerous Liasons.
The film is long by modern standards and could have run the risk of losing its audience because of its slow pace -- Henry James was never an action writer.
But the combination of Campion's sweeping cinematography and Kidman's acting carry the film well, although it has to be said that as a rounded and paced piece of work the Piano was better.
